title: Preface
summary: NVIDIA Corporation’s Form 10-K cover identifies its fiscal year ended January 26, 2025, corporate and securities details, filing and reporting-status certifications, large accelerated filer status, internal-control attestation, market value and shares outstanding, and proxy-statement material incorporated by reference. The contents list Parts I–IV: business, risks, cybersecurity, properties and legal matters; stock information, management discussion, market risk and financial statements; governance, compensation, ownership and auditor matters; and exhibits, financial-statement schedules, and the Form 10-K summary.

title: Where You Can Find More Information
summary: NVIDIA discloses material investor information through its investor relations website, press releases, SEC filings, public calls and webcasts, and social media (corporate and technical blogs, LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, and X), including company, product, financial, and event updates in compliance with Regulation FD. Videos are also available on YouTube. Social-media posts may be material, so investors should monitor these channels alongside formal disclosures. The channel list may change; these channels are not part of the 10-K and may be updated on NVIDIA’s investor relations website.

title: Forward-Looking Statements
summary: The report cautions that forward-looking statements rely on management’s current beliefs, assumptions, and information; identifiable terms may signal them, but risks and uncertainties can make actual outcomes materially different. Readers should review the Risk Factors section, avoid undue reliance, and understand statements are current only as of the filing date; NVIDIA generally undertakes no duty to update them. “NVIDIA,” “we,” “us,” “our,” and “Company” refer to NVIDIA Corporation and its subsidiaries. “We believe” statements reflect potentially limited or incomplete information, not exhaustive review, and are inherently uncertain.

title: Item 1. Business Our Company

nodes.title: Item 1. Business Our Company (intro)
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its evolution into a full-stack accelerated-computing company, combining GPUs, CUDA, software, networking, and data-center-scale systems for AI, analytics, science, graphics, and industry applications. It explains GPU and AI capabilities, its platform strategy and ecosystem, R&D investment and innovation milestones, and use by cloud providers, enterprises, researchers, gamers, and creators. It gives company history, its Compute & Networking and Graphics segments, and four target markets—Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive—then details Data Center workloads, compute and networking products, customers, partners, and GPU foundations.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Businesses and Markets
nodes.summary: NVIDIA computing supports research and discovery across thousands of applications and powers many leading supercomputers. Its GPUs serve gamers, streamers, creators, and generative AI users; its workstation products support professional design and enterprise AI. The page notes NVIDIA’s founding and incorporation history, then outlines its two reporting segments—Compute & Networking and Graphics—and their products and services. NVIDIA’s integrated platforms combine processors, interconnects, software, algorithms, systems, and services for four key markets: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.

nodes.title: Data Center
nodes.summary: The text outlines NVIDIA’s Data Center, Gaming, and Professional Visualization businesses. Data Center combines GPUs, CPUs, DPUs, networking, optimized software, licenses, and DGX Cloud to accelerate AI, analytics, graphics, and scientific computing across cloud, enterprise, and edge environments; it serves diverse customers and partners, and launched Blackwell infrastructure in fiscal 2025. Gaming covers RTX/GTX GPUs, GeForce NOW, and console offerings, highlighting ray tracing, DLSS, AI applications, and the Blackwell RTX 50 Series. Professional Visualization supports design, manufacturing, and content creation through GPU-optimized software, RTX real-time rendering, and Omniverse for simulations and industrial digital twins.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Computing, Gaming, and Visualization
nodes.summary: Describes NVIDIA’s full-stack data center platform, spanning GPUs, DPUs, CPUs, software, enterprise AI services, DGX Cloud, and the Blackwell architecture. Covers gaming trends, RTX ray tracing and DLSS, AI-enabled PCs, gaming products, and Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 Series advances. Explains professional visualization partnerships and workflows across design, manufacturing, and content creation; RTX real-time rendering; and Omniverse for virtual-world simulation and industrial digital twins.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s Automotive business provides end-to-end AI platforms for autonomous vehicles under DRIVE Hyperion, supporting both fully autonomous driving and driver assistance. It works with hundreds of automotive ecosystem partners. Its unified architecture trains AI models in data centers and runs perception, fusion, planning, and control in vehicles using DRIVE AGX hardware, DRIVE OS, sensors, and modular software for driving, mapping, parking, and in-car experiences. Omniverse-based data-center simulation generates training data and supports testing and validation. The software-defined platform enables continuous development and over-the-air feature updates throughout a vehicle’s life.

nodes.title: Business Strategies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s strategy centers on its unified, full-stack accelerated computing platform across data centers, gaming, visualization, and automotive, with shared GPUs, CPUs, CUDA, and networking. It extends leadership in AI through end-to-end hardware, software, cloud services, developer tools, and education; advances AI-powered graphics, creative tools, virtual worlds, and cloud access; develops DRIVE autonomous-vehicle solutions with partners; and licenses or custom-develops its IP. Sales rely on global partners, technical design support, and developer relationships. Gaming revenue is typically stronger in the fiscal year’s second half, though trends may vary. Manufacturing is fabless and outsourced, letting NVIDIA focus on design, quality, marketing, and support.

nodes.title: Technology, Sales, Marketing, and Seasonality
nodes.summary: The page describes technologies for digital avatars, gaming, creative work, 3D collaboration, and cloud-delivered graphics; NVIDIA’s end-to-end DRIVE solutions for autonomous and electric vehicles; and licensing or custom development of its IP. It explains global sales and partner networks, technical pre-sales support, developer engagement, optimized software tools, and AI training. It notes that desktop gaming revenue typically strengthens in the second half of the fiscal year, though past seasonality may not recur.

nodes.title: Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The company uses a fabless, contract-manufacturing model, relying on ISO-certified suppliers for wafer fabrication, assembly, testing, and packaging to reduce costs and operational risks while focusing on design, quality, marketing, and customer support. It sometimes buys raw materials directly, while suppliers procure most inputs. During growth, it may place early non-cancellable orders, pay premiums, or make deposits to secure components and capacity. It has expanded supplier redundancy, though its supply chain is concentrated in Asia-Pacific, using TSMC and Samsung for wafers; SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung for memory; CoWoS packaging; and Hon Hai, Wistron, and Fabrinet for final-product assembly, testing, and packaging.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The market is intensely competitive, with rapid technological change and evolving standards. Competition depends on performance, product breadth, customer and partner access, distribution, software and API support, manufacturing, pricing, and total system cost. Continued competitiveness requires anticipating demand and delivering quality products reliably at competitive prices; competition is expected to grow, including from lower-priced or higher-performing products, new entrants, and alliances. Competitors include GPU, CPU, DPU, SoC, and accelerated-AI processor suppliers; semiconductor interconnect providers; cloud companies developing in-house solutions; and networking suppliers. Some competitors have greater resources or adaptability. Named competitors include AMD, Huawei, Intel, Alibaba, Alphabet, Amazon, Baidu, Microsoft, Ambarella, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Renesas, Samsung, Tesla, Arista, Cisco, HPE, Lumentum, and Marvell, along with internal teams at system vendors and cloud providers.

nodes.title: Patents and Proprietary Rights
nodes.summary: The company protects its U.S. and international intellectual property through patents, trademarks, trade secrets, confidentiality agreements, licenses, and foreign laws and treaties. Its issued patents expire from February 2025 to June 2045, with additional issued, allowed, and pending patents focused on its products and related technologies. Protection may be weaker in some countries, increasing piracy risk. The company evaluates where to seek formal protection based on manufacturing locations, regional business and technology strategies, the existence and enforcement of IP laws, and commercial significance to itself and competitors. It has licensed third-party technology and expects to continue doing so.

nodes.title: Government Regulations
nodes.summary: The text describes expanding U.S. export controls affecting NVIDIA products and markets since 2022, including China, Russia, parts of the Middle East and other country groups; a 2025 AI Diffusion rule proposing worldwide licensing for specified high-performance chips, systems, software and technology; and risks to sales, competition, inventory, product development, supply chains and automotive business. Other regulations could raise costs or harm results, though compliance has not otherwise materially affected operations to date. NVIDIA outlines ESG oversight and reporting, climate initiatives, renewable-energy and supplier-emissions targets, energy-efficient computing, and its Earth-2 climate digital twin. It also reports about 36,000 employees across 38 countries, human-capital oversight, talent recruitment priorities and a predominantly technical workforce.

nodes.title: Sustainability, Climate, and Human Capital
nodes.summary: NVIDIA says regulatory compliance has not materially affected operations to date, but future rules across numerous areas could raise costs and harm business results. It integrates sustainability and governance principles, with Board oversight and annual program reviews. Climate efforts include tracking impacts and risks, matching electricity use with renewable energy (76% in fiscal 2024; 100% goal from fiscal 2025), engaging suppliers on emissions targets, improving computing efficiency, and developing the Earth-2 climate digital twin. NVIDIA also describes its 36,000-person global workforce, Board oversight of human capital policies, and priorities to recruit, develop, and retain talent.

nodes.title: Recruitment
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its workforce strategy: global technical recruiting, employee referrals, diversity hiring, and a highly technical workforce with many advanced degrees; employee learning, mentoring, tuition support, mobility, engagement feedback, and low turnover; performance-linked equity, broad regional benefits, flexible schedules, and family and crisis support. Its inclusion efforts include equitable hiring and advancement, partnerships, targeted recruiting and development, employee groups, training, and tracking workforce outcomes. Fiscal 2025 demographics are reported, alongside flexible work and quarterly company-wide rest days.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Workforce Development, Benefits, Inclusion, and Flexibility
key_items: Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging at NVIDIA
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes employee learning, mentoring, tuition support, internal mobility, engagement feedback, and 2.5% fiscal 2025 turnover. Compensation includes performance-linked equity, while benefits support health, finances, families, and regional needs. The company promotes diverse hiring and advancement through partnerships, recruiting, development, training, and equity tracking; workforce demographics are reported. Flexible work supports recruitment, retention, caregivers, and engagement, alongside two company-wide recharge days per quarter.

title: Item 1A. Risk Factors

nodes.title: Item 1A. Risk Factors (intro)
nodes.summary: The section warns that known and unknown risks could harm the company’s business, finances, results, reputation, and stock price. Risks include changing market needs and competition; demand forecasting, supply constraints, manufacturing dependence and defects; economic, international, cybersecurity, business-disruption and climate risks; acquisitions, customer and distributor concentration, talent retention, systems changes and earnings volatility; and regulatory, export-control, sustainability, responsible technology/AI, intellectual-property, and data-privacy and security challenges.

nodes.title: Industry, Market, and Supply Risks
key_items: Risks Related to Our Industry and Markets
Risks Related to Demand, Supply, and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: The page summarizes risks from changing industry needs and competition; demand forecasting, manufacturing lead times, supply and component availability, reliance on third-party manufacturers, and product defects; and broader global-business risks, including economic and international exposure, cybersecurity and operational disruptions, climate change, investments and acquisitions, customer and distributor concentration, talent retention, business-process and systems interruptions, and fluctuating results that could lower the stock price. Unknown or currently immaterial risks may also cause harm.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock, and Other Matters
nodes.summary: The text outlines regulatory, legal, stock, and other risks, including complex and changing laws and export restrictions; scrutiny of sustainability and responsible technology use, including AI; challenges protecting intellectual property; privacy and cybersecurity obligations; tax liabilities and law changes; litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings; and Delaware law, governing-document provisions, and the Microsoft agreement that could delay or prevent a change in control.

nodes.title: Risk Factors
nodes.summary: Rapid technological, customer, competitive, and standards changes threaten results if NVIDIA cannot adapt products and strategy, invest in R&D, launch software, services and cloud models, expand its ecosystem, meet safety, security, reliability and compliance expectations, manage product lifecycles, secure scalable infrastructure and energy, integrate acquisitions, and fund related operations and sales. R&D in unfamiliar markets may take years to yield revenue or fail; design wins are lengthy, uncertain, and no guarantee of sales or future wins. DGX Cloud depends on partners and multiyear agreements whose timing can shift, affecting revenue, costs, and development, and may not succeed. Standalone offerings such as AI Enterprise, Omniverse, and DRIVE may incur substantial costs without meaningful adoption or revenue.

nodes.title: Competition could adversely impact our market share and financial results.
nodes.summary: Competition in changing markets may intensify as offerings, standards, customer needs, entrants, and industry consolidation evolve. Competitors may offer cheaper or better products, reducing demand and prices, and may benefit from in-house fabrication, stronger IP, more customers and design wins, longer experience, and greater resources. They could capture share, exploit new markets and trends faster, transition products sooner, and constrain access to foundry capacity and scarce materials. Customers may develop substitutes internally; competing cloud AI services could also limit growth. Failure to compete could reduce demand and prevent meaningful revenue or sufficient scale.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply, and Manufacturing Long manufacturing lead times and uncertain supply and component availability, combined with a failure to estimate customer demand accurately, has led and could lead to mismatches between supply and demand.
nodes.summary: Long production lead times, supply constraints, and inaccurate or volatile demand forecasts can cause shortages or excess inventory, harming revenue, margins, customer relationships, and market share. Risks include costly or insufficient capacity commitments, customer order changes, supplier price increases, cancellations, write-downs, and impairments. Demand is affected by economic, technological, competitive, policy, infrastructure, channel, AI, and end-user factors, as well as disasters and geopolitical tensions. Expanding suppliers, products, and prepaid commitments add supply-chain complexity. Frequent product and architecture transitions can disrupt demand, production, quality, and revenue. Emerging or speculative uses, including generative AI and cryptocurrency mining, and gray-market resale further complicate forecasting and may depress prices or demand.

nodes.title: Dependency on third-party suppliers and their technology to manufacture, assemble, test, or package our products reduces our control over product quantity and quality, manufacturing yields, and product delivery schedules and could harm our business.
nodes.summary: The company relies on third-party foundries and subcontractors to manufacture, assemble, test, and package products, limiting its control over supply, quality, yields, and delivery. Risks include supply shortages or decommitments, inaccurate demand forecasts and higher costs, inadequate materials or capacity, process-technology failures, regulatory or policy noncompliance, concentrated suppliers, supplier replacement and integration challenges, unqualified product changes, competitors receiving priority, noncancellable or prepaid orders, low yields, longer lead times, and disruptions from natural disasters, energy conservation, pandemics, or cyberattacks. These risks could impair demand, operations, margins, revenue, and financial results.

nodes.title: Defects in our products have caused and could cause us to incur significant expenses to remediate, which can damage our reputation and cause us to lose market share.
nodes.summary: Complex hardware, software, services, and AI offerings may contain defects, vulnerabilities, failures, or biased outputs, especially with new products and partner-supplied components; problems may emerge after shipment. They can cause data exposure, customer or product damage, recalls, warranty and liability costs, inventory write-offs, diverted staff, regulatory fines, lost market acceptance and design wins, reputational harm, and reduced revenue and margins. A fiscal 2023 defect in a third-party component in Data Center products led to a net warranty liability and may raise future costs; estimates could be insufficient. Product claims may be costly even when third parties are responsible, and insurance may be inadequate or unavailable.

nodes.title: Adverse economic conditions may harm our business.
nodes.summary: Economic, industry, policy, geopolitical, and financial uncertainty—including recessions, inflation, tariffs, supply-chain disruptions, and banking instability—could raise costs, reduce margins and demand, disrupt suppliers and customers, impair forecasting and competitiveness, increase insolvency, credit, collection, borrowing, and liquidity risks, and affect obligations across the company and its counterparties. The company’s investment portfolio, mostly U.S. government securities, is exposed to credit, liquidity, market, and interest-rate risks; prolonged market declines or a U.S. government credit downgrade could weaken the dollar, raise rates, reduce liquidity, and cause investment losses or impairment charges.

nodes.title: International sales and operations are a significant part of our business, which exposes us to risks that could harm our business.
nodes.summary: International sales and outsourced semiconductor manufacturing expose the business to global risks. In fiscal 2025, 53% of revenue came from outside the U.S.; China is highly competitive, with offerings constrained by export controls. Economic and political conditions, lockdowns and public health issues, differing IP and employment laws and business practices, capital-market disruptions, anti-inflation policies, currency fluctuations, natural disasters, war, terrorism, trade restrictions, and other catastrophic events could materially harm business, financial condition, and results.

nodes.title: Product, system security, and data protection incidents or breaches, as well as cyber-attacks, could disrupt our operations, reduce our expected revenue, increase our expenses, and significantly harm our business and reputation.
nodes.summary: Cybersecurity incidents—including increasingly sophisticated malware, ransomware, AI-enabled, geopolitical, insider, and supply-chain attacks—could disrupt operations, reduce revenue, raise costs, and damage the company’s reputation. Recovery, prevention, detection, and remediation may be difficult or delayed, despite ongoing security investment and training. Dependence on suppliers, cloud services, and potentially flawed or biased AI training data creates additional risks, while compromised products could affect many customers. Breaches could expose sensitive information and partner game source code, leading to liability, litigation, regulatory action, disclosure obligations, operational and financial losses, customer attrition, and negative publicity; external sources may also reveal sensitive business information.

nodes.title: Business disruptions could harm our operations, lead to a decline in revenue and increase our costs.
nodes.summary: Disruptions from natural or man-made disasters, infrastructure and supplier failures, cyberattacks, conflict, political instability, regulatory changes, and other events could interrupt global operations, raise costs, reduce revenue, and harm results. Concentrated operations and suppliers in California, Asia, and Israel heighten exposure; geopolitical tensions may affect markets, trade, staffing, and profitability. The company monitors the Israel conflict, which has not caused significant impact so far, though employee military absences and escalation could disrupt development and operations. Reliance on third-party cloud, data center, and other services adds outage and insolvency risks; water, energy, land, and permitting constraints may also limit customers’ data center expansion. Continuity plans may prove insufficient.

nodes.title: Climate change may have a long-term impact on our business.
nodes.summary: Climate change may disrupt the company, its customers, partners, suppliers, and infrastructure through extreme weather, water or energy shortages, wildfire-related power shutoffs, supply-chain impacts, and political instability, increasing attrition, losses, and operating costs. Insurance may be unavailable, insufficient, or exclude losses. Climate laws, regulations, litigation, and stakeholder expectations may raise compliance, energy, manufacturing, capital, and supply-chain costs; require operational or product changes; and cause reputational harm, disputes, or failure to meet sustainability goals. Concerns about GPUs’ high absolute energy use may also hurt business despite their relative efficiency.

nodes.title: We may not be able to realize the potential benefits of business investments or acquisitions, and we may not be able to successfully integrate acquired companies, which could hurt our ability to grow our business, develop new products or sell our products.
nodes.summary: Acquisitions and strategic investments may fail to deliver expected benefits, hinder growth and product development or sales, and harm financial results. Risks include delays, regulatory conditions or approval failures, missed opportunities, lost talent, changing technology, reduced future dealmaking ability, illiquid or unsuccessful investments, impairment losses, and industry concentration. Transactions can divert resources, produce poor returns, face financing, consent or legal obstacles, or evade due diligence. Integration risks include systems, technology, operations, accounting, personnel, liabilities, goodwill and asset write-downs, cybersecurity, and damaged employee, vendor or customer relationships. Financing may increase debt, interest and covenant constraints or dilute equity; consideration may vary, and economic changes may hurt value. Past systems integration difficulties have caused costs, delays, and operational impacts that could continue.

nodes.title: We receive a significant amount of our revenue from a limited number of partners and distributors and we have a concentration of sales to customers who purchase directly or indirectly from us, and our revenue could be adversely affected if we lose or are prevented from selling to any of these customers.
nodes.summary: The text warns that revenue is concentrated among a small number of direct and indirect customers, partners, and distributors, creating risks from lost or reduced orders, channel or system-integration problems, customer or partner strategy changes, trade restrictions, cancellations, and collection or credit constraints. It also describes risks from failing to attract, retain, motivate, or smoothly transition executives and skilled employees; ERP and information-system changes disrupting operations, controls, or financial reporting; material control weaknesses harming investor confidence, finances, and market access; and operating-result volatility, including risks tied to multiyear development spending and contractual obligations.

nodes.title: Partner, Talent, and Systems Risks
key_items: If we are unable to attract, retain and motivate our executives and key employees, our business may be harmed.

Our business is dependent upon the proper functioning of our business processes and information systems and modification or interruption of such systems may disrupt our business and internal controls.
nodes.summary: The company depends on partners and indirect customers for sales, exposing it to changing purchasing patterns, integration challenges, customer concentration, credit constraints, trade restrictions, and collection risks. Its success also depends on attracting and retaining skilled employees and executives amid intense competition, compensation pressures, immigration constraints, and succession risks. Business processes and information systems, including ERP implementation and financial controls, may be disrupted or costly to update; implementation failures or material control weaknesses could impair operations, reporting, investor confidence, stock value, and access to capital, or trigger restatements and regulatory action.

nodes.title: Our operating results have in the past fluctuated and may in the future fluctuate, and if our operating results are below the expectations of securities analysts or investors, our stock price could decline.
nodes.summary: Operating results have fluctuated and may continue to do so, so past performance is not a reliable guide to future results. Risks include multi-year product development and spending adjustments, customer contract compliance and payment collection, extended payment terms and bad debts, credit insurance availability, vendor payment demands, environmental liabilities, and accounting changes. These factors may hinder expected results, constrain cash for operations, and make profitability volatile or unsustainable. Missing company or market expectations could cause the stock price to fall or become substantially more volatile.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock and Other Matters We are subject to complex laws, rules, regulations, and political and other actions, including restrictions on the export of our products, which may adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: The text details risks from complex and changing domestic and international laws, regulatory scrutiny, and compliance costs, including competition, privacy, cybersecurity, AI, sustainability, and product rules. It emphasizes geopolitical tensions, sanctions, and shifting U.S. and foreign export controls—especially restrictions on AI chips and the 2025 AI Diffusion rule—that may limit markets, disrupt supply and operations, raise costs, encourage competitors, and reduce revenue. It also covers Chinese government actions and supply risks, sustainability-related scrutiny and liability, responsible-AI reputational and legal risks, and intellectual-property litigation that may cause damages, injunctions, or impair competition.

nodes.title: China Market, Sustainability and AI Risks
key_items: Increased scrutiny from shareholders, regulators and others regarding our corporate sustainability practices could result in additional costs or risks and adversely impact our reputation and willingness of customers and suppliers to do business with us.
Issues relating to the responsible use of our technologies, including AI in our offerings, may result in reputational or financial harm and liability.
nodes.summary: Chinese gaming and platform restrictions, procurement preferences, product standards, and possible limits on supplies from Taiwan and South Korea could hurt revenue and operations. Sustainability scrutiny may increase compliance costs, liability, and reputational risk, and affect customer and supplier relationships. Responsible-use concerns and evolving AI laws may raise costs, constrain products and operations, slow adoption, and cause competitive, financial, reputational, or legal harm.

nodes.title: Actions to adequately protect our IP rights could result in substantial costs to us and our ability to compete could be harmed if we are unsuccessful or if we are prohibited from making or selling our products.
nodes.summary: Protecting intellectual property can be costly, and failures or restrictions on making and selling products could harm competitiveness. Infringement claims and lawsuits may generate substantial legal costs, management and staff distraction, damages, invalidated patents, lost-profit payments, indemnification obligations, or injunctions. Enforcing IP may raise expenses and trigger countersuits; infringement may require licenses, royalties, cross-licenses, or product suspension if acceptable terms cannot be reached, harming business and results. Protection relies on patents, trademarks, trade secrets, agreements, licenses, and local laws; weaker foreign protections increase piracy risk. Theft, disclosure, or employee moves to competitors may undermine competitiveness, product acceptance, and the value of investments. Applications for formal protection may be denied or unenforceable.

nodes.title: We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security laws, rules, regulations and other obligations. These areas could damage our reputation, deter current and potential customers, affect our product design, or result in legal or regulatory proceedings and liability.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from extensive, evolving privacy, security, AI, and data-protection obligations worldwide. U.S. state and federal laws, including the CCPA, grant consumer rights and impose safeguards and fines; EU and U.K. regimes, the EU AI Act, and NIS2 carry significant compliance duties and penalties. Cross-border transfers and localization rules, especially in Europe and China, may be challenged or require approvals, raising costs and disrupting operations. Contractual duties, customer data breaches, and inaccurate privacy or compliance claims may trigger litigation or enforcement. Changing interpretations and failures by the company or its partners could require product and system changes and lead to fines, restrictions, remediation costs, reputational harm, or material business and financial damage.

nodes.title: We may have exposure to additional tax liabilities and our operating results may be adversely impacted by changes in tax laws, higher than expected tax rates and other tax-related factors.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from tax audits, complex and changing U.S. and international tax rules—including FDII and OECD Pillar One and Two—and other factors that could raise tax rates, costs, and liabilities or harm financial results. It describes ongoing litigation and regulatory exposure, including a securities class action, and potential costs, penalties, injunctions, or disruption. It explains how Delaware law, corporate governance provisions, and Microsoft’s Xbox agreement may impede a change in control. Unresolved staff comments are not applicable. Cybersecurity risk management includes security frameworks and external advice, integrated risk processes, training and policies, and supplier assessments and controls.

nodes.title: Tax, Litigation, and Change-of-Control Risks
key_items: Our business is exposed to the burden and risks associated with litigation, investigations and regulatory proceedings.
Delaware law and our certificate of incorporation, bylaws and agreement with Microsoft could delay or prevent a change in control.
nodes.summary: The text describes tax-rate risks from changing tax laws, accounting, business structure, stock-based compensation, and stock-price volatility. It explains that litigation, investigations, and regulatory proceedings—including a securities class action concerning channel inventory and cryptocurrency-mining GPU demand—may cause costly disruption, fines, damages, injunctions, or other adverse outcomes. Delaware law, corporate governance provisions, and Microsoft’s rights under the Xbox agreement may also discourage or delay takeovers and limit shareholder influence.

summary: The section describes risks that could harm NVIDIA’s business, financial condition, results, reputation, or stock price: rapid technological, market, customer, standards, and competitive changes; uncertain demand, long manufacturing lead times, supply and component constraints, reliance on third parties, product defects, and emerging-product adoption; economic, international, geopolitical, cybersecurity, operational, climate, and energy risks; acquisitions, customer and channel concentration, talent retention, systems and controls, and earnings volatility. title: Critical Accounting Estimates
key_items: Income Taxes; Revenue Recognition Revenue Allowances; License and Development Arrangements
summary: The text explains that U.S. GAAP financial reporting relies on estimates, with critical estimates covering inventory, income taxes, and revenue recognition. The Supreme Court dismissed NVIDIA’s certiorari petition, and the Ninth Circuit judgment took effect, returning the securities case to district court. A California derivative case remains administratively closed; two Delaware federal cases have a 30-day stay extension and a joint status report deadline; and a Delaware Chancery case remains stayed pending the securities case’s resolution. Claims include fiduciary breaches, unjust enrichment, insider trading, corporate waste, and Exchange Act violations; plaintiffs seek unspecified damages, disgorgement, and governance reforms. NVIDIA has accrued no related liabilities because losses are reasonably possible but not probable, and estimates cannot be made; it expects other ordinary-course legal actions will not materially harm its financial condition or results.

The Plan lets eligible employees of the Company and designated companies buy stock and aims to retain, recruit, and motivate employees. It may establish procedures and subplans for foreign or non-U.S. employees, including rules on eligibility, contributions, accounts, currency, taxes, beneficiaries, withholding, and share issuance. nodes.summary: Eligible employees enroll through Company forms, with contributions subject to Board limits and Offering rules; contributions may be adjusted or made by other approved methods, are held in bookkeeping accounts, and earn no interest unless law requires. Participants may withdraw, receiving unused contributions and ending that Offering’s purchase right; rights also end upon loss of employment or eligibility. Rights are personal and generally nontransferable. On purchase dates, contributions buy shares subject to limits and price; residual balances may roll over or be refunded depending on whether they can buy a share and future eligibility. Purchases require securities registration and legal compliance, with delays capped at 27 months, after which contributions are refunded if requirements remain unmet. The Company will seek necessary regulatory approvals unless unreasonable or commercially unavailable. It may allow beneficiary designations, changes, and transfers of shares or contributions upon a participant’s death.

nodes.title: Purchase Rights and Company Covenants
nodes.summary: Purchase Rights are exercisable only by the Participant and generally nontransferable; Contributions earn no interest unless required by law. On Purchase Dates, accumulated Contributions buy shares subject to Plan and Offering limits, with no fractional shares unless allowed. Small leftover balances may roll into the next Offering; larger balances, or balances for ineligible or withdrawing Participants, are refunded without interest. Exercise requires effective securities registration and legal compliance; purchases may be delayed up to 27 months, after which Contributions are refunded if requirements remain unmet. The Company will seek necessary regulatory approvals unless costs are unreasonable, and may be relieved of liability if commercially reasonable efforts fail.

nodes.title: 10. Designation of Beneficiary.
nodes.summary: The text covers beneficiary designations, which the Company may permit participants to submit or change on its approved forms, and how shares or contributions are distributed after death if no valid designation exists. It describes Board adjustments to plan securities and purchase rights after capitalization changes, and treatment of rights in corporate transactions. It sets out Board authority and stockholder-approval limits for amendments, suspension, and termination; protections for outstanding rights and compliance-related exceptions; and begins stating intended Section 409A exemptions for rights under the 423 and Non-423 Components.

nodes.title: Plan Adjustments and Governance
key_items: 11. Adjustments upon Changes in Common Stock; Corporate Transactions.
12. Amendment, Termination or Suspension of the Plan.
nodes.summary: If a participant dies without a valid beneficiary designation, shares and contributions go to the estate’s executor or administrator, or, if none is known, to a person selected by the Company. Capitalization adjustments proportionately revise plan limits, offering and purchase rights, prices, and ongoing purchase limits, as determined finally by the Board. In a corporate transaction, rights may be assumed, continued, or replaced; otherwise, contributions buy shares shortly before closing and rights then terminate. The Board may amend, suspend, or terminate the Plan, subject to required stockholder approval for specified material changes. Suspension or termination stops new rights, while existing rights are protected from material impairment except with consent or as needed for legal, regulatory, listing, or favorable tax compliance, including Section 423.

The Plan’s history, purpose, transition from the 1998 plan, and Section 423 and Non-423 components are described alongside Board and Committee administration, international subplans, and the share reserve. The section covers Offerings and Purchase Rights, eligibility and limits, enrollment, contributions, purchase prices, share allocation, withdrawal, termination, refunds, legal compliance, and beneficiaries. It also addresses adjustments for capitalization changes and corporate transactions, amendment, suspension, and termination authority, protections for outstanding rights, and intended tax treatment.

nodes.title: 13. Code Section 409A; Tax Qualification.
nodes.summary: The 423 Component purchase rights are intended to be exempt from Section 409A, while Non-423 rights for U.S. taxpayers are intended to qualify for the short-term deferral exception; rights subject to 409A will be administered for compliance when the Board determines this applies. The Company disclaims liability and any guarantee of favorable tax treatment, retaining freedom to act despite tax effects. The Plan’s effective date and required shareholder approval are specified. Miscellaneous provisions address proceeds, when share ownership rights begin, no employment contract or change to at-will employment, California governing law, and severability. The text defines the 423 Component as the Plan portion granting qualifying employee stock purchase rights, excluding the Non-423 Component.

nodes.title: Tax Compliance, Plan Effective Date, and Miscellaneous Terms
nodes.summary: The Plan addresses Section 409A compliance and short-term deferral treatment for eligible Purchase Rights, while disclaiming any guarantee of favorable tax treatment or liability for tax outcomes. It takes effect on the Effective Date, but exercises require timely stockholder approval. Share-sale proceeds become Company funds; ownership rights begin when shares are recorded. The Plan and Offering do not alter at-will employment or require continued employment, are governed by California law, and remain effective if an individual provision is invalid.

nodes.title: 16. Definitions.
nodes.summary: Defines terms for NVIDIA’s amended 2012 Employee Stock Purchase Plan, including its 423 and non-423 components, company and participant roles, eligibility, contributions, offerings, purchase rights and periods, stock valuation, corporate transactions, capitalization adjustments, and relevant laws and trading days. The insider-trading policy applies globally to employees, directors, contractors, consultants, and trading proxies, warning about household trading. It defines material nonpublic information (MNPI), gives examples, prohibits trading while possessing MNPI, tipping, derivatives, hedging, shorting, margin purchases, pledging shares, and unauthorized disclosures. Designated Individuals face quarterly trading blackouts; Legal may impose special restrictions. Existing Rule 10b5-1 plan trades are excepted. Policy ownership, dates, and scope are stated.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Insider Trading Policy
key_items: ADDITIONAL RESTRICTIONS APPLICABLE TO “DESIGNATED INDIVIDUALS” ONLY
nodes.summary: The policy covers NVIDIA employees, board members, contractors, consultants, and trades made on their behalf; household and family trading can create legal risk. It defines material non-public information (MNPI), explains materiality and public release, and lists examples. It prohibits trading while possessing relevant MNPI and tipping others. At all times, it bans NVIDIA derivatives, hedging, shorting, margin purchases or holdings, pledging securities, and unauthorized disclosures to the press or financial community. Designated Individuals face quarterly closed-window trading and gifting restrictions, except under qualifying 10b5-1 plans. Legal may impose special restrictions on anyone exposed to risky non-public information, barring NVIDIA trades until notified they end.

nodes.title: EXCEPTIONS
nodes.summary: The policy exceptions permit pre-existing 10b5-1 plan trades, automatic RSU tax withholding and ESPP participation during MNPI possession or closed windows; broadly diversified exchange-fund investments require advance Legal approval. Single-stock exchange-traded products count as trading in the underlying company, while mutual funds and non-single-stock products containing NVIDIA stock are allowed. Gifts are permitted only for estate planning, with beneficial ownership retained, recipient policy compliance, and no reason to expect a prohibited sale. Section 16 directors and officers need Legal preclearance for all NVIDIA stock transactions. Violations may bring legal penalties, including fines or imprisonment, and employment discipline up to termination. Potential violations can be reported to Legal or anonymously via Speak Up/EthicsPoint; NVIDIA seeks confidentiality and prohibits retaliation for good-faith reports or cooperation. Contact Legal with questions before trading or sharing potential MNPI.

nodes.title: Insider Trading Policy: Exceptions, Compliance, and Reporting

Section 16 directors and officers need Corporate Legal preclearance for stock transactions. Violations can lead to fines, imprisonment, and employment or engagement termination. Potential violations can be reported confidentially, including anonymously, through Speak Up; good-faith reporters and investigators are protected from retaliation. Contact Corporate Legal with questions before trading or sharing potential MNPI. The policy applies globally; Legal owns it, last updated February 20, 2025, effective September 22, 2021.
